title: Why Noting Without Stop
paragraphs: *Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammā sambuddhassa* — homage to the Buddha, the blessed, noble and fully self-enlightened one.

Just a quick note about the technique. In the strict Mahāsi tradition one doesn't stop noting. The reason for that is that that which is noting is the discerning mind. For those of you who know your *khandhas*, that's the *viññāṇa*. It's the mind that is able to distinguish between black and white and know what something is for. It's the higher faculty of the mind.

It works on basic perceptions, basic cognitions. It uses words, it uses concepts, it uses images, but mainly it uses words, thinking. At first, when the beginner starts the Mahāsi, it's up front in your face — it's like you're watching yourself, all you're aware of are these words coming out of your head. Then as you keep displacing your attention on feeling, on sensation, the word recedes or becomes like a quiet note in the background.

As you then begin to settle in on an object, begin to fix in on an object — we were talking yesterday about these two stages of *vitakka-vicāra*, the bee flying around the flower and the bee landing. As you're noting, the bee is flying around the flower, and then suddenly you find yourself landing on the flower. The noting again might seem to get in the way, so the meditator stops the noting, and before long they're wandering again because the landing on the flower has not matured.

If you say to yourself, "My attention is steady" — like that's a thought that arises, "I'm really steady on the rising and falling of some object" — and you keep noting, that noting now becomes automatic. Sometimes you might find it more skillful not to note so much what it is you're experiencing, but the process of experiencing. Instead of saying something like "pain, pain," or it might even be a subtle sensation for which there's no word, you might use the word "feeling." You're using the word "feeling" to describe what it is you're actually feeling.

But at that point, it's often more skillful to describe what you're actually doing, which is feeling the object. When you say "feeling, feeling," you're driving your attention closer and closer, more steady on the object in the act of feeling. You're actually feeling. Because this *satipaññā*, this awareness, intuitive intelligence, intuitive awareness, has the ability not only to understand, to observe at that level, but also directly feels, directly experiences.

At that point, when that bee really sticks to the flower, you may be surprised to find that this very noting mind distances itself, so that there's quite a clear separation between the knowing and the noting. This noting carries on because it's been conditioned to carry on discerning. Just like when you've learnt to walk, and now when you walk across the road you don't have to be aware of your legs — the legs just do it. This discerning mind keeps discerning, and you're aware of the object and this discerning mind. But the discerning mind is still helping you, still keeping you on the object. See, still keeping you there.

In the classic Mahāsi teaching you don't stop, because at some point that bee begins to so suck the nectar that it loses itself in the nectar and there's — it sounds a bit dramatic — a collapse. There's a complete joining of this *satipaññā* with what it's actually experiencing, at which point this thinking mind shuts down. At that point this *satipaññā* is at its purest — not that insights can't come before that, but at this point it is extremely pure, and it's not something you can manufacture.

You can get yourself to that point by just diligently noting and diligently guiding your attention to the object. You can't make it collapse, because that collapse is a non-self experience. It's beyond your power. As soon as you say, "Let it collapse," there's somebody there saying, "Let it collapse." You can't do it. That has to happen naturally.
